September 28, 2026 | 2:15 PM
PHILADELPHIA, Sept. 28 –
On Friday evening, New Leash on Life USA held a dog adoption event at Philadelphia Brewing Company which kicked off with state Rep. Joe Hohenstein presenting a $150,000 check to New Leash.

The program rescues at-risk dogs and works with justice-involved individuals in both prison and community settings to create fresh starts.
“The world is a better place when people get second chances. The same is true for our canine companions,” said Hohenstein, D-Phila. “I am proud to support New Leash on Life, which gives those second chances. Their programs provide skills, connection and dignity to people involved in the criminal justice system and dogs caught in shelters with no future in sight. The results speak for themselves as prisoners and pitbulls share the pursuit of happiness and community.”
Marian Marchese, founder and CEO of New Leash on Life USA, expressed the organization’s gratitude to the legislators who fought for this funding.

We continue to expand the number of people and dogs served as well as enhance the skills, knowledge and opportunities offered. We believe in the power of fresh starts - and the participants and rescue dogs at SCI Chester are accomplishing extraordinary success.”

Harris emphasized New Leash’s critical work providing second chances.

They require support, skills and real opportunities,” Harris said. “This $150,000 investment will help prepare people returning home from the justice system to build stable, productive futures while also giving rescue dogs the care and training they need to find loving homes. It is a powerful program that changes lives on both ends of the leash.”

Rep. Gina H. Curry
September 16, 2026 | 1:09 PM
UPPER DARBY, Sept. 16 –
State Rep. Gina H. Curry, D-Delaware, today announced nearly $1.4 million in state funds were awarded to four projects in her district of Delaware County.
The grants awarded include:
$700,000 for the Darby Creek Joint Authority to rehabilitate a portion of the sanitary sewer system in Lansdowne.
$300,000 for the Phase II renovation of the Historic Lansdowne Theater.
$276,173 to replace the roof and HVAC system of the East Lansdowne Administration Building and Community Center.
$100,000 to clean and inspect the storm sewer in Millbourne.
“My team and I are always working diligently to bring state funding to our district and ensure that improvements like these keep our systems running smoothly,” said Curry. “In addition to the sewer improvements, I’m excited to see the Lansdowne Theater continue its renovation and for the East Lansdowne Community Center to get these much-needed upgrades.”
The grants come from
Local Share Account
funds which are approved and distributed by the
Commonwealth Financing Authority

PA Black Maternal Health Caucus chairs reflect on 10 years of the Black maternal health movement
Rep. Gina H. Curry
September 15, 2026 | 3:08 PM
HARRISBURG, Sept. 15
–
After attending the Black Maternal Health Conference 2026, the Pennsylvania Black Maternal Health Caucus co-chairs shared updates on maternal health care efforts and the PA MOMNIBUS 2.0 legislative package.
State Reps. Morgan Cephas, D-Phila.; Gina Curry, D-Delaware; and La’Tasha Mayes, D-Allegheny, appeared on a panel at the conference on Friday, September 11. Led by the Black Mamas Matter Alliance, this year’s theme was “Rooted in Justice & Joy: 10 Years of Building the Black Maternal Health Movement.”
The co-chairs shared the progress of PA MOMNIBUS 2.0, a comprehensive legislative package that addresses critical disparities in maternal health care and includes measures that would improve access to essential services and eliminate maternal health deserts. Curry’s bill package, Expanding Midwifery Access & Authority for Healthier Communities, was recently signed into law by Gov. Josh Shapiro.
“It was an honor to speak on the panel and celebrate 10 years of the Black Maternal Health Movement,” said Cephas. “I am so proud of the progress our movement has made and the solutions we’ve helped deliver to families across the Commonwealth.
“However, there is still more work to do. The fact remains that, in Pennsylvania, more than 90% of pregnancy-related deaths are preventable. And Black women continue to face a dramatically higher risk of dying from pregnancy-related causes. As we celebrate progress, we need to continue fighting to ensure more Black mothers survive pregnancy, receive the care they deserve and come home to their families. I remain focused on advancing solutions that make Pennsylvania a safer and healthier place for mothers, babies and families, and on continuing the great relationships with advocates on the ground that have made this work so meaningful and impactful in Pennsylvania and beyond.”
“Last week’s conference highlighted years of advocacy, expertise and lived experience brought forth by people who are deeply connected to the fight against preventable pregnancy-related deaths, and I was proud to sit on this panel with my colleagues, Representatives Cephas and Mayes, to talk about what we’re doing to move the needle in Pennsylvania,” said Curry. “We are keenly aware that not all states have the political atmosphere to advance legislation like ours. But we hope that one day Pennsylvania will be looked to as an example of success for all mothers and babies.
“The PA Black Maternal Health Caucus will continue to advance legislation that improves outcomes for growing Pennsylvania families and to use our voices in venues like this conference to share our knowledge, lessons and experiences.”
“It was powerful to reflect on 10 years of advocacy to advance Black maternal health nationally and to showcase the groundbreaking work of the PA Black Maternal Health Caucus,” said Mayes. “Our work is rooted in a clear vision: to end preventable maternal mortality and ensure every mother and birthing person has access to the resources they need to have a healthy and joyful pregnancy and birth journey.
“PA MOMNIBUS 2.0 builds on the progress we have made while tackling the gaps that still exist in our health care systems -- including maternal health deserts, midwifery modernization and breastfeeding access -- that still leave too many families without the care they need.
“We have proven that when we listen to communities and turn their experiences into policy, we can save lives. We will continue that work until every family in Pennsylvania has the opportunity to thrive.”
The PA Black Maternal Health Caucus was formed in 2023 by co-Chairs Cephas, Curry and Mayes. The caucus is focused on boldly addressing the disturbing trends of Black maternal mortality and morbidity in Pennsylvania through strategic, intersectional legislation and evidence-based policy solutions. Four MOMNIBUS bills have been signed into law since the initiative was launched in 2024.

September 11, 2026 | 3:02 PM
UPPER DARBY, Sept. 11 –
State Rep. Gina H. Curry, D-Delaware, invites girls in grades four through eight to join her for the 5th annual Inspi-HER’d Field Day for Girls, happening 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 26 at Naylor’s Run Park.
Inspi-HER’d is a FREE celebration of wellness and empowerment that creates a joyful space for girls to be themselves, try something new, build confidence and connect with other girls while exploring what it means to be well in mind, body, relationships and community.
“Every girl deserves a space where she feels seen, supported and encouraged to shine,” Curry said. “Inspi-HER’d is about surrounding our girls with positive experiences and people who remind them that they are strong, capable and full of possibility and having a whole lot of fun while we do it!”
Girls can look forward to an action-packed afternoon featuring dancing, martial arts, Zumba, interactive wellness activities, community resources, special guests, prizes and more. Lunch also will be provided.

Delaware County legislators’ statement on threats to Sheriff Kamara
Rep. Gina H. Curry
July 29, 2026 | 9:37 AM
UPPER DARBY, July 29 –
The Delaware County House Delegation today released the following statement on the race-based threats received by Delaware County Sheriff Siddiq Kamara:
“The Delaware County House Delegation unequivocally condemns the recent terroristic threats directed at Delaware County Sheriff Siddiq Kamara. There is no place for intimidation, violence or hate against those who choose to serve and live in any community in our county and the state.
“Public servants regardless of political party, position or ideology should never be subjected to threats of violence for carrying out their sworn responsibilities, or for their faith, background or culture. An attack or threat against one public official is an attack on the principles of democracy, public service and the rule of law that bind our Commonwealth together.
“As members of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, we stand in unwavering solidarity with Sheriff Kamara, his family and the dedicated professionals of the Delaware County Sheriff’s Office. We also stand with Delaware County's diverse communities, including our vibrant immigrant communities, who deserve to live free from fear, hate and intimidation. Rep. Gina H. Curry
July 15, 2026 | 3:19 PM
HARRISBURG, July 15 –
On Sunday, the General Assembly passed legislation that will streamline fetal death paperwork for families who experience loss during a midwife-led birth. The bill, introduced by state Rep. Gina H. Curry, D-Delaware, now heads to the governor’s desk to be signed into law.
“
This is an important moment for families who choose to have midwife-led birth journeys, or who have limited access to medical doctors because of where they live and the strength of their local healthcare system,” said Curry. “Right now, midwives are not allowed to sign required fetal death reports after a stillbirth delivery or infant death during birth. That means families are being forced to wait through an overly bureaucratic process while they grieve.”
Under current law, if a death certificate is needed and no qualifying professional was present during the delivery, the case must be referred to the county coroner for investigation. Qualifying professionals include physicians, certified nurse practitioners, or physician assistants.
According to Curry, adding midwives to this list not only streamlines the process, but also alleviates an emotional burden for families while recognizing the professional skills midwives bring to the birthing process.
“Imagine going into labor only to experience the death of your expected child and then being asked to sit back and wait while the county coroner investigates the passing, simply because you chose to work with a midwife instead of a doctor,” said Curry. “These families are already in a state of emotional distress. Midwives are highly trained, compassionate medical professionals, and there’s no reason they can’t complete this process for their patients.
“I am proud of our state legislature and my colleagues on both sides of the aisle for seeing the value in this important change to our laws. Together, we are making a difference for families at one of the most vulnerable moments of their lives.”

initiative and is the second midwifery bill from that package to reach the governor’s desk. With its enactment, House Bill 1851 becomes the fourth

Bill directing state education secretary to assess Keystone Exams passes Pa. House
Rep. Gina H. Curry
May 4, 2026
HARRISBURG, May 4 –
State Rep. Gina H. Curry, D-Delaware, today announced that her legislation pushing for a Keystone Exam Alternative Feasibility Study passed the Pennsylvania House of Representatives by a bipartisan vote of XX to XXX.
Should the state Senate also pass H.B. 1752, the Pennsylvania Department of Education secretary would be tasked with contracting an independent study to determine whether the academic SAT, ACT, and Smarter Balanced high school assessments could be used in place of the 11
th
grade Keystone Exams in Pennsylvania.
“Since 2012, the Keystone Exams have helped schools and the state and federal government keep track of student subject competency and teaching accountability,” Curry said. “They have also had many pros and cons, and this bill’s intent is to alleviate some of those cons.”
According to Curry, one downside to assessments such as the Keystone Exams is the cost of administering them to students. In 2019, a report by the state Auditor General found that while the Keystone Exams cost approximately $17.6 million annually to administer and score for all high school juniors, the cost of administering and scoring the SAT for both juniors and seniors was only $13.3 million per year.
“Like the Keystones, the SAT and other college-readiness tests assess student competency of certain subjects – these tests are all largely looking at the same type of metrics, even if they’re scoring them somewhat differently,” Curry said. “If schools had the flexibility to offer their students the SAT or ACT instead of Keystones, that’s a significant savings. Half of our students already choose to take the SAT or ACT as part of their college application process.”
Under the bill, the independent study would assess:
The degree to which the ACT, SAT and Smarter Balanced tests align with the Keystone Exams.
How well the results of these exams provide comparable assessment of student achievement, compared to the Keystone Exams.
Whether these exams can accommodate students with disabilities and English learners as well as the Keystone Exams.
Whether using these tests would meet existing state and federal requirements.
A cost-comparison of using these tests in place of the Keystone Exams.
In addition, the state education secretary would be responsible for submitting a report that details how the department and schools would transition to a new testing protocol, how results would be reported, and more.
“We all know education evolves as we learn more about student success and as the world changes,” Curry said. “Considering changes to our standardized testing practices should be part of that evolution, too.”
The bill now heads to the Senate for consideration.

HARRISBURG, April 28 –
To recognize the historic and ongoing contributions of the Delta Sigma Theta sorority, four alumnae of the sorority, state Reps. Lindsay Powell and La’Tasha D. Mayes, both D-Allegheny, Gina H. Curry, D-Delaware, and Morgan Cephas, D-Phila., hosted Delta Day in the state Capitol today.
Delta Day is celebrated by
Delta Sigma Theta Sorority Inc.
, which was founded in 1913 by 22 collegiate women on the campus of Howard University. Today, Delta Sigma Theta Sorority Inc. is one of the preeminent service-based sororities, with more than 300,000 predominantly Black members and more than 1,000 chapters worldwide. The sorority has maintained a commitment to social activism, academic excellence and civic engagement.
Delta Sigma Theta Sorority Inc. has 29 chapters in Pennsylvania. On Delta Day, members from throughout the Commonwealth come to the Capitol to connect with elected officials, advance legislation and serve as a voice for others.
“It was an honor to welcome sorors from across Pennsylvania to continue our long history of sisterhood, service and leadership to advocate for our communities,” Powell said. “Having even just one voice at the table can be powerful, but the hundreds of us here today prove that our lifelong service to our communities will continue.”
“As a proud member of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority Inc., I am deeply honored to stand alongside everyone here at the Capitol for Delta Day,” said Mayes. “Our sorority has always been rooted in uplifting our communities through sisterhood, scholarship, service and social action, and today is a reminder that our work continues both inside and outside the Capitol. Together, we are celebrating our 113-year legacy and we are actively shaping a more just future for all Pennsylvanians.”
“For the past 113 years, the women of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority Inc. have been a driving force behind civic engagement, community change, social activism and the elevation of Black women nationwide,” Curry said. “Communities are built and sustained on the bonds of this kind of sisterhood, and I am proud to be part of this family and to welcome our illustrious organization and sorors to the Capitol today.”
“I am so proud to celebrate my 20th year as a Delta,” Cephas said. “It is always an honor to co-host Delta Day at the Capitol with Reps. Mayes, Curry and Powell. This day ensures Deltas connect with lawmakers to discuss pressing issues facing our communities. This is how we build on our founders’ legacy of promoting academic excellence and providing assistance to those in need. I’m so proud of what we’ve accomplished as an organization and how we continue marching forward. Through our service, the next generation can inherit progress, not the same fights we are facing today.”
The four lawmakers, this year led by Cephas, have introduced
H.R. 469
, a resolution that recognizes and celebrates Delta Day and the sorority’s work. The legislation awaits consideration in the full House.

Bill allowing nurse-midwives to refer patients for pelvic floor therapy passes Pa. Senate, heads to governor’s desk
Rep. Gina H. Curry
April 22, 2026 | 11:40 AM
HARRISBURG, April 22 –
The Pennsylvania Senate today passed legislation by state Rep. Gina H. Curry, D-Delaware, that will make it easier for more women to access pelvic floor therapy. The bill now heads to the governor’s desk.
House Bill 1251 would amend the Physical Therapy Practice Act to allow nurse-midwives to refer their patients for pelvic floor therapy, streamlining the process for their patients.
Under current law, only physicians, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants can refer patients for pelvic floor therapy, a type of physical therapy that addresses pelvic floor issues including pain, incontinence, and abdominal muscle problems common after pregnancy and childbirth. This means patients who choose to use a nurse-midwife for obstetric care first need to see one of these approved practitioners before they can get a referral for pelvic floor therapy.
“Midwives provide competent, compassionate care to thousands of women each year, and for too long we’ve overcomplicated certain processes by not recognizing their profession as equal to other pre- and post-natal providers,” said Curry. “When a woman chooses to work with a midwife on her birth journey, she should have the same ease of access to related wellness care as a woman who chooses a doctor.”
According to Curry, pelvic floor therapy can allow women experiencing pelvic heaviness, pelvic pain, urinary leakage, and organ prolapse to improve their condition with specialized exercises so that they can avoid invasive surgeries.
The bill is half of a two-part bill package focused on the role of midwives during pregnancy and childbirth, and is part of the PA Black Maternal Health Caucus’
MOMNIBUS 2.0 comprehensive legislative package
confronting Black maternal mortality and morbidity in Pennsylvania.
“I am deeply grateful to my peers in the legislature for seeing the value in this bill, and to all of the grassroots organizations that have been advocating for the highest level of care for all mothers on their birthing journey,” said Curry. “We’ve met this goal because of all of them.”
The American Midwifery Certification Board reports that in 2025, 590 certified nurse midwives work in Pennsylvania; current research shows that anywhere from 25% to 50% of women will experience a pelvic floor issue in the 10 years after giving birth.
House Bill 1251 passed the Senate 45-2, after passing the House in December.

Lawmakers demand more action after shocking testimony
Testimony underscores disparities for Black moms, need for legislation
Rep. Gina H. Curry
April 14, 2026 | 3:29 PM
HARRISBURG, April 14 –
After being discharged from the hospital while in labor, Mercedes Wells shared how she gave birth along a road in a Chevrolet Silverado after her health concerns were dismissed by health care professionals.
At a House Majority Policy Committee hearing hosted by the Black Maternal Health Caucus, lawmakers highlighted the disparate outcomes facing Black mothers, who are
three times more likely to die
from pregnancy-related causes than white mothers.
“This is not a hearing about a single point of failure,” said state Rep. Morgan Cephas, who co-chairs the Black Maternal Health Caucus and represents portions of Philadelphia. “This hearing amplifies the layered challenges across the entire continuum of maternal care—from implicit bias in clinical settings to limited access to prenatal and postpartum services to maternity care deserts in too many communities. The challenges are systemic. No family in Pennsylvania should be forced to worry about losing their life due to pregnancy complications or living with lasting effects because of a failed system.”
A recording of the hearing’s livestream can be found
here
.
“Black mothers face higher risks, and that is unacceptable,” said state Rep. Gina H. Curry, who co-chairs the Black Maternal Health Caucus and represents portions of Delaware County. “We need a fundamental shift in how the health care system listens to its patients and cares for Black mothers before, during, and after pregnancy. Every mother deserves safe, respectful, and high-quality care. The time to act is now.”
The
CEO at the hospital
that discharged Wells acknowledged she was discharged moments before giving birth, publicly apologized, promised policy changes and cultural competency training for staff, and noted a doctor and a nurse lost their jobs.
“Black moms are not always heard, and too often, the consequences can be tragic and deadly,” said state Rep. La’Tasha D. Mayes, who co-chairs the Black Maternal Health Caucus and represents portions of Allegheny County. “Until all lawmakers prioritize targeted legislation, this crisis will continue. That’s why I am introducing the Pennsylvania WELLS Act to keep hospitals accountable for the care they provide.”
The
PA Momnibus 2.0
is a comprehensive legislative package consisting of 12 bills, including five bills that have already passed the House.
“Today’s hearing is about ensuring every mother is heard, respected, and cared for throughout her pregnancy and beyond,” said PA House Democratic Policy Committee Chairman Ryan Bizzarro, who represents portions of Erie County. “We have the tools to make a difference and the legislation to save lives.”
More than 80% of pregnancy-related deaths in the U.S. are preventable, according to the CDC, recognizing the importance of warning signs, timely treatment and quality care. In October 2024, Gov. Josh Shapiro signed two key components of the
first PA Momnibus package
into law, including Medicaid reimbursement for doula services and a statewide public awareness campaign on postpartum depression.
Information about this hearing and other House Majority Policy Committee hearings can be found at
pahouse.com/policy
. Photos to be used for publication can be found at
https://www.facebook.com/PADemPolicy
.

Democratic SE Delegation urges PUC to reject PECO rate hikes
Letter to PUC chair cites ‘significant financial hardships’ on ratepayers
Rep. Gina H. Curry
April 8, 2026 | 1:06 PM
HARRISBURG, April 8 —
Members of the Pennsylvania House Democratic Southeast Delegation today wrote to the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission to express their strong opposition to proposed gas and electric rate hikes by PECO, according to state Rep. Jennifer O’Mara, D-Delaware, the delegation chair.
PECO last week filed a request with the PUC to significantly increase gas and electric rates beginning next year. On average, these rate hikes would cost families an additional $20.08 per month for electricity and $14.52 per month for natural gas.
In the joint letter to PUC Chair Steve DeFrank, the legislators spelled out their concerns that “PECO’s habitual requests for rate increases over the last few years are excessive, and that this rate increase in particular will benefit for-profit large load users at the expense of Pennsylvania’s long standing residential customers and small businesses.
“Many of those who live and work in Southeast counties are concerned about the significant financial hardships that the proposed rate increase would create, given that, if approved, this would be PECO’s third rate hike since 2022,” the letter continued.
The Democratic Southeast Delegation includes House members from Bucks, Chester, Delaware and Montgomery counties.
In addition to urging the PUC to reject the rate increases, the delegation members asked the commission to hold four public hearings on the proposals, one in each of Philadelphia’s collar counties.
“Holding local hearings will allow for greater accessibility and transparency for our constituents, who deserve to be a part of this process,” the legislators wrote.

Bill streamlining post-stillbirth paperwork passes Pa. House unanimously
Rep. Gina H. Curry
March 26, 2026
HARRISBURG, March 26 –
Families who experience loss during a midwife-led birth could soon avoid the added trauma of completing fetal death paperwork thanks to legislation introduced by state Rep. Gina H. Curry, D-Delaware, that passed House unanimously yesterday.
“Right now, only a physician, certified nurse practitioner, or physician assistant can complete required fetal death reports after a stillbirth delivery or infant death during birth,” said Curry. “But many families choose to have midwife-led deliveries during which these professionals are not on hand. In these cases, the process of completing the death certificate becomes a significant emotional burden for grieving parents.”
Allowing certified midwives to complete and sign fetal death certificates would streamline the process and allow grieving families to move forward. Under current law, if a death certificate is needed and no qualifying professional was present during the delivery, the case must be referred to the county coroner for investigation.
“Imagine going into labor only to experience the death of your expected child and then being asked to sit back and wait while the county coroner investigates the passing, simply because you chose to work with a midwife instead of a doctor,” said Curry. “These families are already in a state of emotional distress. Midwives are highly trained, compassionate medical professionals, and there’s no reason they can’t complete this process for their patients.”
The American Midwifery Certification Board reports that as of 2025, there were 590 certified nurse midwives working in Pennsylvania.
H.B. 1851 now moves to the state Senate for consideration.

PA House designates January 23, 2026 ‘Maternal Health Awareness Day’
Rep. Gina H. Curry
February 4, 2026 | 1:19 PM
HARRISBURG, Feb. 4 —
State Rep. Gina H. Curry, D-Delaware, celebrated the adoption of a resolution (H.R. 379) designating Jan. 23, 2026 “Maternal Health Awareness Day” in Pennsylvania.
Curry, a co-founder of the Pennsylvania Black Maternal Health Caucus, said the resolution is designed to raise awareness of critical issues surrounding maternal health and the wellbeing of mothers and infants across the state.
“An alarming number of people are still unaware of the maternal health crisis we face in Pennsylvania and nationwide,” said Curry. “We are encouraging residents and health care providers to get educated about this issue and learn how they can better care for themselves, their children, their families, and their neighbors.”
House Resolution 379 was co-sponsored by state Reps. Morgan Cephas, D-Phila., and La’Tasha D. Mayes, D-Allegheny, also co-founders of the PA Black Maternal Health Caucus. The PABMHC works to advance legislation that improves health outcomes for mothers and infants.
The resolution was adopted yesterday by a vote of 168-29.

Effort to enact 'Marnie's Law' launches in General Assembly
Named for actor Marnie Schulenburg, H.B. 2850 would require education about deadly breast cancer
Rep. Gina H. Curry
October 19, 2026 | 3:40 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 19 —
A new effort was launched in Pennsylvania today to enact “Marnie’s Law,” which would require healthcare providers to be educated on the deadly cancer that killed Emmy-nominated actor Marnie Schulenburg.
State Reps. Jennifer O’Mara, D-Delaware, Bridget Kosierowski, D-Lackawanna, and Gina Curry, D-Delaware, announced the introduction of
H.B. 2850
at a news conference in the state Capitol along with Schulenburg’s father, widower, daughter, and other relatives.
Marnie Schulenburg, best known for her role on “As the World Turns,” died in 2022 of inflammatory breast cancer, or IBC, an aggressive form that is often overlooked and misdiagnosed as mastitis. She was diagnosed with IBC five months after giving birth to her daughter in December 2019.
“Marnie never gave up as she fought cancer, but the cancer never gave up. And I won’t either, and neither will everybody up here,” said John Schulenburg, her father.
O’Mara said supporters of Marnie’s Law met today with state Senate President Pro Tempore Kim Ward, R-Westmoreland, as they began laying the groundwork to move the legislation through the General Assembly.
“Because we understand that breast cancer does not care about your party,” O’Mara said. “It doesn’t care about what chamber you’re in or what state you live in, and we want to make sure here in Pennsylvania that we are doing everything we can to fight for women and to make sure their providers are educated.”
Schulenburg’s widower, Zack Robidas, noted that Schulenburg went public with her story on social media before she died “because she wanted other women to know what she hadn’t known.
“We’re here to continue what Marnie started. We’re here to get more women more time,” Robidas said.
Kosierowski, who was recently diagnosed with breast cancer, pointed out a sign behind her during the Capitol press conference that said, “Stop Cancer When It’s Curable.”
“And that’s really the meaning behind this legislation, and the meaning behind what Marnie fought so hard for,” Kosierowski said.
Curry, co-chair of the Pennsylvania Black Maternal Health Caucus, noted that more than 13,700 Pennsylvanians are expected to be diagnosed with breast cancer by the end of this year, and more than 1,770 are expected to die from the disease. IBC accounts for up to 5% of breast cancers, and Black women have an IBC incidence rate more than 70% higher than that of other women.
“Recognizing this disease is not just an awareness issue; it is an issue of timely diagnosis, health equity and potentially lifesaving action. That is why Marnie’s Law matters,” Curry said.
More information
about “Marnie’s Law” is available here:
Home - Marnie's Army

PBMHC applauds Shapiro’s Launch of First Apprenticeship Program to Train Doulas
Rep. Gina H. Curry
October 22, 2026 | 9:42 AM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 21 –
Following Gov. Josh Shapiro’s
establishment of the nation’s first doula apprenticeship program
, Pennsylvania Black Maternal Health Caucus co-chairs and state Representatives Morgan Cephas, D-Phila., and Gina Curry, D-Delaware, released a statement to express their gratitude and support. The program will expand Pennsylvania’s maternal health workforce and increase access to doulas.
“For years, research has shown us that doula support leads to improved birth outcomes and reduced complications. Doulas provide continuous support throughout pregnancy and the important first year following, contributing to safer and more positive experiences for families," Cephas said.
"However, this care means nothing for families who cannot access it. We see a vast disparity in care for women who are already statistically at risk for adverse pregnancy outcomes, with Black birthing people at the highest risk of maternal and infant mortality and morbidity compared to other racial and ethnic groups.
“By removing barriers to becoming a doula, this apprenticeship program will expand access to a proven network of support, leading more families to better health outcomes during the birthing journey. I am grateful to Governor Shapiro for establishing this landmark apprenticeship program and continuing to invest in maternal health.”
“This apprenticeship program is poised to significantly improve the birth experience for expecting moms throughout our state,” said Curry. “Doula care means access, advocacy, and allyship that adds the support delivering moms need. When we give women the support they need to stay healthy and strong in pregnancy, we see better birth outcomes. This is huge news for the women of Pennsylvania. In maternal health care deserts, like our rural areas and areas like Delaware County, this will add accessibility and increased resources that are desperately needed.”
The Pennsylvania Statewide Registered Doula Apprenticeship Program was established in a collaboration among the Pennsylvania departments of Human Services, Health, and Labor and Industry, and Patients R Waiting.
This is the Shapiro administration’s latest measure to expand access to doulas. In 2024, the governor signed into law Act 115, legislation sponsored by Cephas which extended Medicaid coverage to doula services.
The Pennsylvania Black Maternal Health Caucus, which recently celebrated its three-year anniversary as a caucus, was formed by Cephas and Curry, and State Rep. La’Tasha Mayes, D-Allegheny. PBMHC is a bicameral group composed of over 50 legislators focused on boldly addressing the disturbing trends of Black maternal mortality and morbidity in Pennsylvania through strategic, intersectional legislation and policy. DCIU provides important resources and programs for Delaware County, supporting students, families, and educators across the region. Ensuring the integrity of its administrative and fiscal operations is essential to preserving that mission and maintaining public trust. Administrative and fiscal practices that ensure the DCIU remains a good steward of commonwealth resources, and delivers on its mission, are critical.
We encourage the DCIU and the Auditor General’s office to continue working together and to act promptly on the recommendations that are expected following the completion of this process. Delaware County taxpayers deserve clarity on how public funds are being used, and transparency will be critical as these matters are addressed.
We appreciate the Auditor General’s work in conducting this audit and bringing these matters to light. We remain committed to ensuring that taxpayer resources are used responsibly and in accordance with state law, and we will continue proactive efforts to ensure that the DCIU is following the appropriate financial, administrative, and transparency requirements expected of any public entity.
